title: Proactor Pattern
oneLiner: Hands the entire I/O operation to the OS and gets notified only when it's fully complete — no readiness polling required.

hero.name: The Delegate
hero.catchphrase: Don't wait for it to be ready — hand it off, and I'll tell you when it's DONE.
hero.power: Delegates the actual I/O operation to the OS/runtime, freeing the calling thread entirely until a completion notification arrives.
hero.weakness: True async I/O completion support isn't available everywhere, and completion-based code can be genuinely harder to reason about than simple readiness-based code.
hero.origin: The Delegate appeared inside a file-processing service where the Reactor pattern still required the app to actively read once notified — an extra step that async disk I/O could skip entirely.

story.problem: A Reactor-based file service gets notified when a file descriptor is 'readable', then still has to perform the actual read itself — an extra round-trip that, for disk I/O, the OS could have done directly.
story.solution: The Delegate hands the OS the entire read operation upfront — buffer and all. The OS performs it asynchronously and notifies the app only once the data is fully copied into the buffer.
story.result: The app thread never touches the read operation itself. It submits the request once and reacts only to a 'here's your finished data' notification.

before: App is notified when I/O is merely ready, then must perform it itself
An extra read/write call happens on every I/O readiness event
The app thread does real work for every I/O operation
after: App submits the operation once; the OS performs it entirely
The app is notified only when the operation is fully complete
The app thread does no I/O work itself — just handles the result

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A profiler shows the app performing a read() call immediately after every single readiness notification, every time.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Every readiness event is immediately followed by us calling read() ourselves. Couldn't the OS just do the whole thing and tell us when it's done?

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Delegate appears holding a sealed package, handing the entire task to a courier.
panels.speaker: The Delegate
panels.dialogue: Don't wait to be told 'it's ready to read'. Hand the WHOLE operation to the OS — I'll tell you the moment it's actually finished.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: readAsync(buffer) submits the entire operation to the OS. A completion handler fires only once the buffer is fully filled.
panels.speaker: The Delegate
panels.dialogue: You never call read() yourself. The OS performs it entirely and hands you the finished buffer through the completion callback.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: The redundant read() call disappears entirely from the app's hot path.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: The app thread doesn't touch the I/O operation at all anymore. It just reacts to finished results.

useWhen: The platform provides true asynchronous I/O completion (Windows IOCP, io_uring on Linux, or a runtime built on them).
You want to eliminate the extra 'notified ready, then perform the operation' round-trip that Reactor requires.
I/O throughput at scale matters enough to justify the added complexity of completion-based programming.
avoidWhen: The platform doesn't support efficient async I/O completion — a hand-rolled Proactor may perform worse than a well-tuned Reactor.
The added complexity of completion-based (vs. readiness-based) reasoning isn't worth it for your actual I/O volume.
Your runtime's async I/O abstraction already handles this for you (many modern async runtimes blend Reactor and Proactor internally).
commonMistakes: Assuming Proactor and Reactor are interchangeable — mixing readiness-based and completion-based assumptions in the same codebase causes subtle bugs.
Not handling partial completions or errors in the completion callback, assuming every operation always fully succeeds.
Overestimating platform support — true async I/O completion isn't uniformly available across every OS and file/network I/O type.
Building a hand-rolled Proactor when the runtime (like .NET's async I/O or a modern async runtime) already provides one, tested and tuned.
explanation.realWorldExample: Windows I/O Completion Ports (IOCP), Linux's io_uring, and .NET's asynchronous file/socket APIs are real-world Proactor implementations, often abstracted away by higher-level async/await runtimes.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: How is this actually different from Reactor? Both feel 'asynchronous'.

conversation.speaker: The Delegate
conversation.message: The difference is WHO does the I/O. Reactor tells you 'this is ready — go read it yourself'. I perform the entire read for you and only notify you once it's genuinely finished.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: So why isn't everyone always using you instead of Reactor?

conversation.speaker: The Delegate
conversation.message: Because true async completion needs real OS support — IOCP, io_uring — which isn't uniform everywhere. Reactor's readiness model is simpler and more portable, which is exactly why it's so much more common.

codeBattle.scenario: Your high-throughput file-processing service on Windows needs to issue thousands of disk reads per second with minimal thread overhead, and the platform offers native async I/O completion support (IOCP).
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Delegate lets the OS perform each read entirely via IOCP, notifying the app only on completion, avoiding both thread-per-read overhead and the extra readiness-then-read round-trip.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between Proactor and Reactor?
options: Proactor is notified when an I/O operation is fully complete; Reactor is notified when I/O is merely ready to be performed
They are exactly the same pattern
Reactor requires more threads than Proactor in every case
Proactor can only be used for network I/O, never disk I/O
quiz.answer: Proactor is notified when an I/O operation is fully complete; Reactor is notified when I/O is merely ready to be performed
quiz.explanation: This readiness-vs-completion distinction is the defining difference between the two patterns.

quiz.question: What does the calling thread do in a Proactor-based read?
options: Submits the operation once, then does nothing until a completion notification arrives
Continuously polls the file descriptor for readiness
Performs the entire read itself, synchronously
Spawns a new thread for every byte read
quiz.answer: Submits the operation once, then does nothing until a completion notification arrives
quiz.explanation: The whole point of Proactor is that the calling thread never performs the I/O operation itself.

quiz.question: What limits Proactor's applicability in practice?
options: True asynchronous I/O completion support isn't uniformly available across every OS and I/O type
It can only be used with exactly one file at a time
It cannot be combined with async/await
quiz.answer: True asynchronous I/O completion support isn't uniformly available across every OS and I/O type
quiz.explanation: Mechanisms like IOCP and io_uring exist, but aren't as universally available as basic readiness notification (used by Reactor).

quiz.question: What's a real-world example of the Proactor pattern?
quiz.explanation: IOCP is a textbook OS-level Proactor implementation, notifying applications only once an I/O operation has fully completed.
